sources.ref_file_title: KZG10 - Constant-size commitments to polynomials and their applications
sources.authors: Aniket Kate, Gregory M. Zaverucha, Ian Goldberg
sources.note: Existing wiki reference page; key reused verbatim.

pages.class_justification: The security proof is a standard straight-line reduction (the evaluation-binding adversary is run once as a black box and its two conflicting openings are algebraically transformed into a q-SDH solution), but the RTV04 class vocabulary is defined for primitive-from-primitive constructions: here the hypotheses are an assumption plus a group structure used concretely, not primitives accessed as oracles, so no RTV04 class is honestly assignable. KZG10 does not classify the reduction.
pages.model_justification: The scheme requires a trusted structured reference string $(g, g^\tau, \ldots, g^{\tau^d})$ generated with a secret $\tau$ that must be discarded; this is a structured-CRS setup, matching the page's current model value.
pages.statement: In a bilinear group with a trusted structured reference string $(g, g^\tau, \ldots, g^{\tau^d})$, the KZG scheme is a [[polynomial-commitment|polynomial commitment]] for polynomials of degree at most $d$: commitments and opening proofs are single group elements, verification is two pairings, and evaluation binding holds under the [[q-strong-diffie-hellman|$q$-SDH]] assumption with $q = d$ [[KZG10 - Constant-size commitments to polynomials and their applications|KZG10]].
pages.sketch: Commit to $f$ as $C = g^{f(\tau)}$, computable from the SRS without knowing $\tau$; the opening at $z$ is $\pi = g^{\psi(\tau)}$ for the quotient $\psi(X) = (f(X) - y)/(X - z)$, and the verifier checks $e(C/g^y, g) = e(\pi, g^\tau/g^z)$. Two accepting openings $(y, \pi) \neq (y', \pi')$ at the same point $z$ yield $(\pi/\pi')^{1/(y'-y)} = g^{1/(\tau - z)}$, a $q$-SDH solution.
notes_to_keep: The bilinear-group requirement is a structural hypothesis: `[[pairings]]` is a Glossary page, not an assumption page.
flags: Migration Notes claiming 'q-Strong Diffie-Hellman has NO assumption page' are stale: content/Assumptions/q-strong-diffie-hellman.md now exists (stub, unlisted). The dangling-hypothesis notes can be dropped.
Pseudocode is the non-hiding PolyCommit_DL variant of KZG10; the hiding variant (PolyCommit_Ped) adds a Pedersen blinding polynomial. The wiki's PCS syntax (Setup, Commit, Open, Vrfy) is followed.
Efficiency bullets (O(1) proof, two-pairing verification) are folded into the statement so nothing from the migrated quote is lost.

sources.ref_file_title: Gro16 - On the Size of Pairing-based Non-interactive Arguments
sources.note: Existing wiki reference page. Abstract verified via web search: pairing-based preprocessing SNARK for arithmetic circuit satisfiability, 3-group-element proofs, single pairing-product-equation verification, EUROCRYPT 2016 pp. 305-326.

sources.ref_file_title: FKL18 - The Algebraic Group Model and its Applications
sources.authors: Georg Fuchsbauer, Eike Kiltz, Julian Loss
sources.note: Existing wiki reference page; proves knowledge soundness of Groth16 in the algebraic group model under a q-type discrete-logarithm assumption.

pages.class_justification: Knowledge soundness is proven only against generic adversaries; per schema/reduction-classes.yaml the idealized model goes on the model axis with class: free (a proof in the GGM restricts the adversary, not the reduction technique). Matches the page's current value.
pages.model_justification: Gro16 proves knowledge soundness of the construction in the generic bilinear group model. The scheme additionally requires a per-circuit trusted CRS, which the single-valued model field cannot also record; the statement text carries it.
pages.statement: Given a [[pairings|bilinear pairing]] and a per-circuit trusted CRS, there is a zk-[[succinct-argument|SNARK]] for arithmetic circuit satisfiability whose proofs consist of three group elements (two in $\GG_1$, one in $\GG_2$) and whose verification checks a single pairing product equation; knowledge soundness is proven in the generic bilinear group model [[Gro16 - On the Size of Pairing-based Non-interactive Arguments|Gro16]].
pages.sketch: The circuit is arithmetized as a quadratic arithmetic program; the CRS contains group encodings of powers of a secret evaluation point, the prover combines them into three group elements encoding the QAP divisibility check, and the verifier checks one pairing product equation. Knowledge soundness holds against generic-group adversaries, whose group operations allow extracting the witness from the proof elements' representations.
pages.improvements_text: - Knowledge soundness of Groth16 is proven in the algebraic group model under a $q$-type discrete-logarithm assumption — [[FKL18 - The Algebraic Group Model and its Applications|FKL18]].
notes_to_keep: INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY on the source page: [[succinct-argument]] elsewhere says '3 $\GG_1$ elements + 1 $\GG_2$ element' (= 4). Groth16 proofs are 2 $\GG_1$ + 1 $\GG_2$ = 3 elements, so that line is the erroneous one. Reported, not fixed.
'pairings' resolves to a Glossary page, not an assumption page — a hypothesis slot filled by a structure.
flags: The hypothesis is a structure (bilinear pairing), with the real cryptographic content in the model axis (GGM). A sibling edge kea-to-snark-gro16 records a knowledge-assumption reading of the same result; a human should decide whether both edges should stand or be consolidated.
succinct-argument.md's '3 G1 + 1 G2' proof-size claim is wrong (Groth16 = 2 G1 + 1 G2 = 3 elements) — skeptical-checker lane, already recorded in this page's Notes.

sources.ref_file_title: BIPW17 - Can We Access a Database Both Locally and Privately
sources.authors: Elette Boyle, Yuval Ishai, Rafael Pass, Mary Wootters
sources.note: Existing wiki reference page. TCC 2017 pp. 662-693; verified via web search: candidate SK-DEPIR from the conjectured hardness of distinguishing a secretly permuted set of Reed-Muller local-decoding queries from uniformly random points.

sources.ref_file_title: BHW19 - Permuted Puzzles and Cryptographic Hardness
sources.authors: Elette Boyle, Justin Holmgren, Mor Weiss
sources.note: Verified at eprint 2019/1256 and Springer DOI 10.1007/978-3-030-36033-7_18. Initiates the formal study of permuted-puzzle problems, the framework capturing the BIPW17 assumption (and the source of this page's hypothesis name).

sources.ref_file_title: BHMW21 - On the Security of Doubly Efficient PIR
sources.authors: Elette Boyle, Justin Holmgren, Fermi Ma, Mor Weiss
sources.note: Existing wiki reference page; cryptanalysis of the DEPIR candidates' assumptions — breaks a proposed generalization, not the core BIPW17 conjecture (per the wiki's own gloss).

pages.class_justification: BIPW17 give a candidate construction whose security is argued directly from a bespoke conjecture about the scheme's own query distribution; the paper does not classify the reduction, and the RTV04 vocabulary (primitive-from-primitive, oracle-access quantifiers) does not cleanly apply to an assumption-based candidate. Honest value: unstated.
pages.model_justification: No idealized oracle or setup beyond the secret key; the conjecture is a standard-model indistinguishability assumption.
pages.statement: Assuming the [[permuted-puzzles|permuted-puzzles]] conjecture of BIPW17 — that a secretly permuted set of Reed–Muller local-decoding queries is indistinguishable from a uniformly random set of points — there is a secret-key [[doubly-efficient-pir|doubly efficient PIR]]: the database is preprocessed once into a polynomial-size encoding, after which the key holder retrieves any bit by reading a small number of positions of the encoding, and the observed access pattern hides the retrieved index [[BIPW17 - Can We Access a Database Both Locally and Privately|BIPW17]].
pages.sketch: The database is encoded as (a noised, secretly permuted copy of) the evaluation table of a low-degree extension; to fetch a bit the client evaluates the polynomial along a random curve through the target point, so its probe set looks like a permuted Reed–Muller decoding query set, which the conjecture makes indistinguishable from random positions.
pages.improvements_text:
- The assumption family is formalized and systematically studied as _permuted puzzles_ — [[BHW19 - Permuted Puzzles and Cryptographic Hardness|BHW19]].
- Later cryptanalysis breaks a proposed generalization of the assumption while leaving the core BIPW17 conjecture standing — [[BHMW21 - On the Security of Doubly Efficient PIR|BHMW21]].
notes_to_keep: 'SK-DEPIR' is an alias of [[doubly-efficient-pir]] rather than a node of its own: the conclusion page is the general DEPIR object while the theorem yields only the secret-key variant.
flags: Migration Notes saying 'No page exists for the assumption' are stale: content/Assumptions/permuted-puzzles.md now exists (stub, unlisted, id bipw17-permuted-puzzles-assumption).
The statement paraphrases the abstract-level guarantee (one-time polynomial-size preprocessing, sublinear per-query reads); exact parameter trade-offs are in BIPW17 and were not pinned down here.

CHR17 (Canetti-Holmgren-Richelson, 'Towards Doubly Efficient Private Information Retrieval', TCC 2017) is a concurrent SK-DEPIR candidate from a related but distinct assumption — a separate edge, deliberately not added here.

pages.class_justification: Proven complexity-class containment; per repo convention the reduction-class axis does not discriminate and the value is free.
pages.statement: Every language in [[bounded-error-probabilistic-polynomial-time|BPP]] has a trivial one-message [[arthur-merlin|Arthur–Merlin]] protocol in which Arthur ignores Merlin's message and runs the BPP decider himself, so $\classBPP \subseteq \classAM$ — folklore.
pages.sketch: An AM protocol with completeness 2/3 and soundness 1/3 in which Merlin's message is discarded is exactly a BPP algorithm, so the containment is definitional.
flags: The current source attribution to GS86 is WRONG and should be removed: Goldwasser-Sipser 1986 proves the private-coin/public-coin equivalence (IP[k] in AM[k+2]); BPP in AM is immediate from the definition of AM and predates any citation — the page's own migration Notes already record this doubt. Disposition folklore, statement ends '— folklore'.
With the GS86 citation dropped, the slug suffix '-gs86' is misleading; renaming the file changes a live URL, so leave the rename decision to a human.

sources.note: Bibliographic data verified via DBLP record journals/siamcomp/BernsteinV97 and the published paper header (SIAM J. Comput. 26(5):1411-1473, 1997) surfaced in web search; the paper establishes BPP ⊆ BQP ⊆ P^#P. doi.org itself is egress-blocked from this environment, so the DOI is the standard recorded one, cross-checked against DBLP.

pages.class_justification: Proven complexity-class containment; per repo convention class: free.
pages.model_justification: The containment is witnessed by a quantum simulation of the probabilistic machine; sibling BQP edges (e.g. bqp-to-pp) use model: quantum, and the page's current value is kept.
pages.statement: A quantum Turing machine simulates any bounded-error probabilistic polynomial-time computation with polynomial overhead, so [[bounded-error-probabilistic-polynomial-time|BPP]] $\subseteq$ [[bounded-error-quantum-polynomial-time|BQP]] [[BV97 - Quantum Complexity Theory|BV97]].
pages.sketch: A quantum machine generates a fair coin by rotating a qubit into an equal superposition and measuring, and executes each deterministic step of the probabilistic machine reversibly, reproducing its acceptance probabilities exactly; BV97 formalize this simulation for quantum Turing machines.
flags: The migrated quote's gloss 'classical probabilistic computation is a special case of quantum computation' is morally right but the containment is a theorem (reversible simulation + coin tosses), first proved for QTMs in BV97 — hence sourced rather than folklore.

pages.class_justification: Proven complexity-class containment; per repo convention class: free.
pages.statement: [[bounded-error-probabilistic-polynomial-time|BPP]] is closed under complement, and every BPP language has a trivial one-message protocol in which Arthur ignores Merlin and decides alone; applying this to the complement language gives $\classBPP \subseteq \classcoAM$ ([[co-arthur-merlin|coAM]]) — folklore.
pages.sketch: $L \in \classBPP$ implies $\bar{L} \in \classBPP \subseteq \classAM$, and $\bar{L} \in \classAM$ is the definition of $L \in \classcoAM$.
flags: Same wrong GS86 attribution as bpp-to-am-gs86: the containment is definitional (BPP closure under complement plus BPP ⊆ AM), not a Goldwasser-Sipser result; drop the citation and label folklore. Slug suffix '-gs86' becomes misleading; renaming is a human call since filenames are live URLs.
This also repairs the migrated 'Symmetrically' clause: the coAM direction is justified by BPP's closure under complement, which the statement now says explicitly.

pages.class_justification: Proven complexity-class containment; per repo convention class: free.
pages.statement: A [[bounded-error-probabilistic-polynomial-time|BPP]] machine accepts yes-instances with probability at least $2/3$ and no-instances with probability at most $1/3$, so it already meets the strict-majority acceptance criterion of [[probabilistic-polynomial-time|PP]]: $\classBPP \subseteq \classPP$ — folklore.
pages.sketch: The bounded-error gap places the acceptance probability strictly on the correct side of $1/2$ on every input, so the same machine is a PP machine verbatim.
flags: Both classes and the containment appear in Gill's SICOMP 1977 paper defining probabilistic complexity classes; the containment is definitional, so folklore is the honest label and no Gil77 reference page is proposed.

sources.ref_file_title: Adl78 - Two theorems on random polynomial time
sources.note: Bibliographic data (19th FOCS 1978, pp. 75-83, DOI 10.1109/SFCS.1978.37) verified via web search. Adleman's theorem; the paper literally proves RP ⊆ P/poly, and the BPP form follows by the same argument after amplification and is universally credited to this paper (e.g. Arora-Barak Thm 7.14). doi.org is egress-blocked from this environment; DOI cross-checked against search results.

pages.class_justification: Proven complexity-class containment; per repo convention class: free.
pages.statement: Every language in [[bounded-error-probabilistic-polynomial-time|BPP]] is decided by a family of polynomial-size Boolean circuits: $\classBPP \subseteq \classPpoly$ ([[p-poly|P/poly]]) [[Adl78 - Two theorems on random polynomial time|Adl78]].
pages.sketch: Amplify the BPP machine's error below $2^{-n}$; a union bound over the $2^n$ inputs of length $n$ shows some single random string is correct on all of them, and hardwiring that string as the advice yields the circuit family. Adl78 proves the $\classRP$ case; the BPP form follows by the same argument after amplification — standard.
flags: Resolves the explicit 'TODO citation (Adleman 1978)' recorded on both source pages; the duplicate justifications on bounded-error-probabilistic-polynomial-time.md and p-poly.md can now cite Adl78.
The p-poly.md quote's derandomization clause (E requires exponential circuits ⇒ BPP = P, Impagliazzo-Wigderson) is a different result and does not belong on this edge.

pages.class_justification: Proven complexity-class containment; per repo convention class: free.
pages.statement: A [[polynomial-space|PSPACE]] machine decides any [[bounded-error-probabilistic-polynomial-time|BPP]] language by enumerating all polynomially long random strings, reusing space across runs, and accepting on the majority outcome: $\classBPP \subseteq \classPSPACE$ — folklore.
pages.sketch: Each of the $2^{\poly(n)}$ runs uses polynomial space and only a counter of accepting runs is kept, so the whole majority vote fits in polynomial space.

pages.wrong_reason: With kind: inclusion, hypothesis bqp, conclusion dlog, the page asserts BQP ⊆ DLOG (its own title says so). This is inverted and type-confused: DLOG is a hardness assumption/computational problem, not a complexity class that could contain BQP. Shor97 proves the opposite-direction fact — the discrete logarithm problem admits a polynomial-time quantum algorithm, i.e. DLOG ∈ BQP, so the DLOG assumption fails against quantum adversaries. The page's own migration Notes record 'POLARITY INVERTED'. The correct edge, if kept as an inclusion, is dlog-to-bqp (hypothesis dlog, conclusion bqp, kind inclusion, model quantum, source Shor97, class free); no such page exists yet. Alternatively, record Shor's algorithm under # Attacks on content/Assumptions/discrete-logarithm.md rather than as a reduction page.
flags: HIGH PRIORITY: page asserts the inverse of Shor's theorem; propose replacing with dlog-to-bqp (DLOG ∈ BQP, Shor97) or an Attacks entry on discrete-logarithm.

The migrated bullet's factoring half ('Integer factorization ... in BQP via Shor') is 'sub-edge 0' per the Notes and is likely recorded elsewhere with the same inversion; no bqp-to-factoring/factoring-to-bqp page exists in content/Reductions at the time of this pass — worth checking where sub-edge 0 landed.
